title: How People Made Sugar Before Modern Factories | Time-Travel Engineering
historical_lens: 1792 Rajahmundry Circar, southeastern India; not a claim of uniform historic technology
footage_disclosure: Modern licensed visual demonstrations; never label any footage as historical film

scenes.title: SUGARCANE BEFORE THE FACTORIES
scenes.narration: In seventeen ninety-two, observers documented sugar making in southeastern India. Cane moved from fertile fields to presses and boiling pans. The footage here is modern, not a recording of the past.
scenes.subtitle: Modern view of a sugarcane plantation

scenes.title: CARRYING THE HARVEST
scenes.narration: Workers harvest sugarcane and carry bundles to processing sites. This modern film shows stalks being carried, not cut. Fresh cane must reach the press promptly so the extracted juice stays usable.
scenes.subtitle: Harvested stalks carried by hand

scenes.title: HOW A PRESS EXTRACTS JUICE
scenes.narration: A press squeezes cane between moving surfaces. Liquid escapes while tough plant fibers remain. Historical hand and animal-powered designs varied. This cutaway explains the force, not one exact eighteenth-century machine.
scenes.subtitle: Compression releases liquid

scenes.title: THE FORCE OF THE PRESS
scenes.narration: This real modern press feeds cane between rollers. The machine shows extraction, not historical refining. The first product is cloudy juice carrying dissolved sugar and plant particles, still far from finished sugar.
scenes.subtitle: Modern real cane press: mechanics shown

scenes.title: FIBERS, JUICE AND LABOR
scenes.narration: Workers guide and handle cane beside active machinery. These are real modern techniques, not a reconstructed old mill. The stalks yield juice, while the fibrous leftovers can be collected separately.
scenes.subtitle: Handling cane beside processing machines

scenes.title: JUICE IS ONLY THE FIRST STEP
scenes.narration: At a modern stall, rollers squeeze fresh cane juice. It may be consumed as a drink, but it is not preserved jaggery. Making a solid sweetener requires clarification and water removal.
scenes.subtitle: Real press; unprocessed juice is perishable

scenes.title: HEAT REMOVES WATER
scenes.narration: Open pans expose sweet juice to heat. Water evaporates, concentrating the dissolved sugar. Dry cane fiber, called bagasse, can fuel a furnace. This animation explains the process, not a specific old kiln.
scenes.subtitle: Evaporation changes concentration

scenes.title: REAL OPEN-PAN BOILING
scenes.narration: Steam rises from real cane juice boiling in an open pan. As water escapes, the syrup concentrates. Workers must control heat and watch the texture. This is modern film of a traditional process.
scenes.subtitle: True boiling cane juice, present-day demo

scenes.title: WATCH THE SYRUP CHANGE
scenes.narration: In this present-day Punjabi workshop, workers stir syrup as it thickens. Evaporation changes its texture and concentration. This authentic craft footage is not an eighteenth-century recording or proof of a universal recipe.
scenes.subtitle: Real traditional jaggery concentration in Punjab

scenes.title: FROM SYRUP TO JAGGERY
scenes.narration: As thick syrup cools, sugar crystals may form within a complex mixture. The result can become brown, semi-crystalline jaggery, also called gur. This illustration does not represent refined white sugar.
scenes.subtitle: Jaggery cooling is not refining

scenes.title: BROWN SUGAR IS NOT JAGGERY
scenes.narration: Here, modern brown table sugar is poured into a jar. It is not jaggery. Brown sugar commonly contains refined crystals and molasses, while jaggery comes from concentrated cane juice. Similar colors conceal different processes.
scenes.subtitle: Modern retail brown sugar — not historical gur

scenes.title: ONE PLANT, MANY TECHNOLOGIES
scenes.narration: Today's powered presses work faster, yet the essential sequence is recognizable: harvest cane, squeeze the juice, concentrate it with heat, then cool. Techniques changed across regions, but people made sweeteners before factories.
scenes.subtitle: Present-day press footage; science is timeless
